introduction: These nineteen passages speak about Christians from outside the churches and, they insist, from inside devotion to Christ. They begin by defending Jesus against the charge that he destroyed the law of Moses, then argue that the churches now repeat the mistake of that earlier generation: reading promises by the letter, waiting for a body to descend from the sky, content with the water already in their vases. The New Testament supplies both the argument and the objection. Jesus said that Elijah had come and was not known, that the letter kills, that he had other sheep not of this fold; but two men in white said he would come as he went, the Apocalypse says every eye shall see him, and he himself warned against anyone who cries “Lo, here is Christ.” Dostoevsky’s Inquisitor and Frederick Douglass, from within Christendom, said harder things about the churches than the readings do.
questions: Jesus said that Elijah had already come in John the Baptist. What does that precedent establish about how promises of return are fulfilled, and what does it leave open?
“This same Jesus … shall so come in like manner”, and “every eye shall see him”. State as fairly as you can why a Christian would take these literally. How do the readings answer?
Jesus warned against false Christs. How can a believer be both obedient to that warning and open to a claim, and what test do the readings imply?

Dostoevsky and Douglass distinguish Christ from the practice of the churches, as reading 4 does. What is gained by that distinction, and what care does it require of those who draw it about another community?

outside.why: The Pharisees fancied Christ an enemy of Moses who destroyed his Law. His own answer in the Sermon on the Mount: think not that I am come to destroy; I am come to fulfil.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá proves the validity of Christ so that Christians may attain his truth. Jesus argued in the same way from the earlier Messenger: had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me.

“If Christ himself were to appear in these temples, the very pillars of the churches would deny Him.” Dostoevsky imagined it: the Grand Inquisitor arrests the returned Christ and asks why he has come to hinder them.

It is unfair to judge Christ by the deeds of Christians. Frederick Douglass drew the same line from inside slavery: between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ, the widest possible difference.
The divines “clung to the literal interpretation of the words of Jesus”. Paul’s own maxim stands against them: the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.

Christians look for fulfilment “according to the letter”. They have a text: this same Jesus shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven. How should a reader of the readings answer the two men in white?
“Just what the Jews did in the time of Jesus.” Elijah was expected from heaven; Jesus said he had come already in John, and they knew him not.
The reading cites this claim: he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man. If “from heaven” was true of one born of Mary, the same phrase need not mean the sky a second time.

The stars and clouds “are but symbols”. The Apocalypse says: he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him. A coming that most do not see is hard to square with this; what would the readings say “see” means?
This is the thirteenth verse the reading means: he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak. The reading argues that only a person hears and speaks.
The Church reads the promise as fulfilled at Pentecost, when they were all filled with the Holy Ghost. Which details of John’s chapter fit that event, and which does the reading say it leaves over?
“We have enough water in our vases.” Jesus on the taste for what one already has: no man having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better.
John the Baptist on the sufficiency of heritage: think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father.
All Christians were praying for the Kingdom, and it came unnoticed. The day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night.

The priests “seek pretexts”. Yet Jesus warned them: if any man shall say, Lo, here is Christ, believe it not; there shall arise false Christs and shall deceive the very elect. Is caution a pretext? What test did he leave?
A book written to mislead, like those written against Christ. Gamaliel’s advice to an earlier council: if this work be of men, it will come to nought; but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
Ninety years of schools and hospitals, and few converts. Jesus on zeal for proselytes: ye compass sea and land to make one.
How can a member of the Church accept this Cause? Other sheep I have, which are not of this fold; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
“Our souls, our hearts, our spirits are sacrificed in devotion to Christ’s station.” Paul’s measure of that devotion: I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ.
